# Task description

> In this task, we are going to use various **supervised learning methods** to try to predict the antibody response to influenza vaccination using early gene expression measurements. The main goal of the practical is to understand the concepts behind **cross-validation** : why we need it, how it works, and how it is used to tune the hyperparameters of a model.

> To save us some time, I have preprocessed the data for you. The data is an extract of open-access data from the Human Immune Project Consortium, with [detail of the study found here](https://immunespace.org/query/study/SDY1119#study-citations). The relevant information for this exercise is as follows :
>
> - Antibodies were measured at days 0 and 28
> - Gene expression of around 10,000 genes was measured at days 0 and 7. To reduce the computation time, I kept only the 1,000 most variable genes

> Flu is an interesting virus in this context, since it is a common disease, and many people may have already been infected with a given flu strain prior to vaccination. There is evidence in the literature that prior infection can modify the response to vaccination. Therefore, to take into account baseline (day 0) information, I have transformed both the response and the predictors into (log2) fold-change values. That is, the *ratio* between the post-vaccination and pre-vaccination measurements.

> Our task will be to see if the day 7 fold-change of expression in some genes is predictive of the day 28 fold-change in antibody levels. That is, we seek to find an early gene expression signature which informs us of the later antibody response.

# Setup

## 0a) Set up your project

### Why do we need a project?

> When you analyse data in R, you need to tell R *where* files are. For example, you might load data into your environment by defining a path `"C:/Users/me/Documents/data/file.xlsx"`. However, this is problematic, since it is specific to your own computer setup. The code will then break as soon as you move the files, share them with a colleague, or re-run the analysis on a different machine.

> To avoid this, we will introduce some basic organisational skills for an R project. Firstly, we will contain the work in a single **R project folder** (the root), and refer to every file *relative to that folder*. This makes specifying paths for loading data and saving outputs more robust.

> Using a project folder also helps to organise files in a clean way.
>
> - **raw data** : the original data files, which you should never modify;
> - **analysis** : the code (such as this `.Rmd` file) that reads the raw data and produces results;
> - **output** : everything the code creates (figures, tables, processed data), which should be able to be perfectly regenerated by re-running the code.

### Create the project folder

> If you already created a project for a previous practical, you can reuse it : open it and go to "Add the files" below. Otherwise :

> 1. In RStudio, click `File > New Project... > New Directory > New Project`.
> 2. Give the project a name, for example `omics_practicals`, and choose where to save it on your computer. Click `Create Project`.
> 3. RStudio restarts inside your new project. You can check this in the top-right corner of RStudio, which now shows the project name, and in the `Files` pane, which shows a single file called e.g. `omics_practicals.Rproj`.

> Next, create three sub-folders inside the project. In the `Files` pane of RStudio, click `New Folder` and create `data-raw`, `analysis`, and `output`. Alternatively, run the following code once in the R console.

```{r, eval = F}
dir.create("data-raw")
dir.create("analysis")
dir.create("output")
```

> Your project should now look like this:

```
omics_practicals/
├── omics_practicals.Rproj    <- marks the "root" of the project
├── data-raw/                 <- the raw data files
├── analysis/                 <- the practicals (.Rmd files)
└── output/                   <- figures and results that you save
```

### Add the files

> 1. Copy the data file I sent you, `SDY1119_day7_GE_foldChange_top1000.RData`, into the `data-raw` folder.
> 2. Copy this practical (the `.Rmd` file) into the `analysis` folder.
> 3. In the `Files` pane of RStudio, open the `analysis` folder and click on the `.Rmd` file to open it.

> **Important:** always start your work by opening the project (double-click the `.Rproj` file, or use `File > Open Project`), and open the `.Rmd` file from *within* RStudio's `Files` pane. If you open the `.Rmd` file directly from your Downloads folder, it will not be part of the project and the paths below will not work.

### How do we refer to files?

> By default, R Markdown runs code from the folder where the `.Rmd` file is saved (here, `analysis/`), which would make paths confusing. Instead, we will use the `here` package. The function `here()` always returns the path to the root of your project (the folder containing the `.Rproj` file), wherever the code is run from. We then build paths from this root. For example, `here("data-raw", "my_file.RData")` points to `my_file.RData` inside the `data-raw` folder, and `here("output", "my_plot.pdf")` points to a file in the `output` folder. The same code works on any computer and operating system, and you never have to type a full path.

# 1) Building a predictive model

> In this section, we are going to demonstrate how to fit a predictive model to a dataset and use it to make predictions. We will demonstrate how fitting a model to a dataset, and making predictions on the same samples used to fit the model, results in over-optimistic evaluation of the prediction error. 

## 1a) Fitting a ridge regression model

> As a first example, we are going to fit a *ridge regression* model to the entire dataset. Ridge is a regularised linear regression with a penalty term controlling the size of the coefficients. It is implemented in the `glmnet()` function of the `glmnet` package, with the argument `alpha = 0`. The strength of the penalty is controlled by the argument `lambda`. For now, we will fix `lambda = 1`. The `glmnet()` function takes the predictors as a matrix `x` and the response as a vector `y`, and predictions can be made with the `predict()` function, giving the predictors as the argument `newx`.

> Fit a ridge regression with `lambda = 1` to all of the observations.

```{r}

```

> Now use the `predict()` function to make predictions of the response, using the same data (`X_mat`) as an input to the `newx` argument. 

```{r}
# Your code here
```

> Now we've made these predictions, we can evaluate them with **performance metrics**. For the purposes of this exercise, we will be using two metrics. The first is the root-mean-squared-error (RMSE) between the true values $y_i$ and the predictions $\hat{y}_i$ :

$$
\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}
$$

> The lower this is, the better. Since we standardised the response, it has a standard deviation of 1, and the RMSE can be read as follows : if RMSE = 1, your predictions are as good on average as a model which simply predicts the average response (i.e. one which does not use any of the predictor information). Anything below 1 indicates a model which predicts better than this naïve model.

> The second metric is the R2 statistic, which is the squared Pearson correlation between the response and the predictions :

$$
R^{2} = cor_{\text{pearson}}(y, \hat{y})^{2}
$$

> The higher this is, the better. It can be interpreted as "the proportion of variability in the true response which is explained by the predictions".

> Below is a helper function which you can use to compute these metrics, by inputting your true and predicted response values. 

```{r}
calculate_metrics <- function(true, predicted) {
  sRMSE = sqrt(mean((true - predicted) ^ 2))/sd(true)
  R2 = cor(true, predicted, method = "pearson") ^ 2
  
  metrics = list("sRMSE" = sRMSE, "R2" = R2)
  
  return(metrics)
}
```

> Compute and report the two metrics for your first ridge regression fit on the entire dataset.

> We could also interpret our predictions by visualising the true versus predicted values. The below helper function allows you to do this, with the arguments being the true values, predicted values, and a string to use as a descriptive title for the figure. 

```{r}
plot_predictions <- function(true, predicted, title = "Insert a descriptive plot title here") {
  # The same limits for both axes : the range of the true and predicted values, with some padding
  results_range <- range(c(true, predicted))
  padding <- diff(results_range) * 0.02
  lims <- c(results_range[1] - padding, results_range[2] + padding)

  ggplot(data.frame(true, predicted), aes(x = true, y = predicted)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 2) +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
    coord_equal(xlim = lims, ylim = lims) +
    labs(title = title, x = "True (observed)", y = "Predicted") +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"))
}
```

## 1b) A training set and a testing set

> The predictions above are made on the data which was used to fit the model, so they say nothing about how the model would perform on new participants. The simplest way to evaluate the model on *unseen* data is a **train-test split**. Observations are randomly assigned to either the training set or the testing set. A model is trained on the training set, and used to predict on the unseen testing set. The predictions can then be compared to their true values to obtain an unbiased estimate of the model's performance.

# 2) K-fold cross-validation

> The train-test split uses the data inefficiently : only 30% of the participants are predicted, and the result depends on the random split. **K-fold cross-validation** is a better alternative. Here, we first split the data into K distinct *folds* (partitions of the data). Cross-validation is a loop, where in each stage, a different fold is chosen to act as the testing set, and a model is trained on all the other folds. Therefore, K-fold cross-validation results in a series of K models, and in a prediction on unseen data for **every** participant. In this section, we are going to improve on our previous train-test split by implementing 10-fold CV.

# 3) Tuning hyperparameters with `caret`

> Some models have *hyperparameters* to specify, which are parameters which control certain aspects of the learning process. Ridge regression, for example, has the hyperparameter **lambda**, which controls the strength of the penalisation term. Since we are unlikely to have much reason to prefer any particular values of these hyperparameters, we may prefer to let the data decide for us which are the *best* values. We can also do this with cross-validation : we try different values of the hyperparameters, and we keep those which give the best predictions (here, the lowest RMSE).

> However, we must be careful. If we choose the hyperparameters using the same predictions that we use to evaluate the model, the performance will be over-optimistic (the same problem we evoked in question 1). Instead, we typically do something called *nested cross-validation* in order to first build a model with optimal hyperparameters, and then use that model to predict on unseen data. A nested cross-validation has two loops. The first, called the *outer loop*, separates the training data from the testing data (which is what you implemented above). The second, called the *inner loop*, uses cross-validation on the training data only to select the best values of the model hyperparameters. The testing data is never used to choose the hyperparameters.

> Coding the inner loop from scratch is tedious, especially when the model has several hyperparameters. Luckily, the `caret` package exists to automate hyperparameter tuning. Caret standardises syntax across packages to allow for many predictive models to be easily implemented. To train models and find the best hyperparameter(s), we use the `train()` function in `caret`. This function takes the following main arguments :
>
> - `x` : the matrix or data frame of predictors (columns) by samples (rows)
> - `y` : the vector of responses
> - `method` : the name of the regression method to be used. A full list of methods implemented in caret [can be found here](https://topepo.github.io/caret/available-models.html). Ridge regression is implemented in `glmnet`, so the method name is "glmnet".
> - `tuneGrid` : a data frame where each column is a named hyperparameter from the method, and each row is a unique combination of these hyperparameters to be used to fit a model to the training data. The `expand.grid()` function creates such a data frame from the values to try for each hyperparameter. For the "glmnet" method, the hyperparameters are `alpha` (0 for ridge regression) and `lambda`.
> - `trControl` : an object created using the `trainControl()` function which defines how the tuning process should be performed. For example, `trainControl(method = "cv", number = 5)` implements 5-fold (inner) CV for deciding the hyperparameters.
> - `metric` : the metric to be optimised when choosing the *best* model. We will use the root mean squared error (`metric` = "RMSE").
>
> The result of `train()` is a model which has been fitted on all the training data with the best hyperparameters. It can be used with `predict()` as before (with the testing predictors as the argument `newdata`), and the best hyperparameters are stored in its element `$bestTune`.

> You are going to add 5-fold hyperparameter tuning in the ridge regression CV you implemented above. All this will require is to replace the call to `glmnet()` above with a call to `caret::train()`, using the arguments `method = "glmnet"`, `tuneGrid = ridge_grid`, and `trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 5)`. As before, you may make predictions in the test set with the `predict()` function. Also, store the tuned values of the hyperparameter **lambda**, extracted from the `bestTune$lambda` of the `caret::train()` object. You may use the grid of hyperparameter options suggested below as inputs (its values are spread over several orders of magnitude, since lambda acts on a multiplicative scale).

```{r}
lambda_grid <- c(0.001, 0.005, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100)

ridge_grid = expand.grid(alpha = 0, lambda = lambda_grid)
```

# 4) Other models

> Now that you have a nested cross-validation framework with `caret`, it is easy to try other models : you only need to change the `method` and the `tuneGrid`. For each of the following models, repeat your code from the previous section (with the same outer folds), and choose the hyperparameter values to try yourselves. Compute the metrics, plot the predictions, and save the figure. To compare the models later, store the predictions and metrics of each model in objects with distinct names (e.g. `pred_lasso` and `metrics_lasso`).

> **How should you choose a hyperparameter grid?** There is no rule, and a grid is always somewhat arbitrary, but here is some practical advice. (1) Start with a small, coarse grid : every extra value multiplies the computation time (the number of models fitted is the number of rows of the grid, times 5 inner folds, times 10 outer folds). (2) For penalty parameters such as lambda, which act on a multiplicative scale, use values spread over several orders of magnitude (e.g. 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10) rather than evenly spaced values. (3) After tuning, look at the selected values (the `$bestTune` of the `train()` object) : if a selected value is at the edge of your grid, the best value may lie beyond it, so extend the grid in that direction. Each model below comes with an example grid to start from.

## 4c) Principal component regression

> Principal component regression (PCR) first computes the principal components of the predictors, and then regresses the response on the first few components. It is implemented in the `"pcr"` method (package `pls`). The hyperparameter to tune is the *number of components to keep*, `ncomp`. Note that it cannot be larger than the number of participants in the training set. For example, you could use the grid `data.frame(ncomp = c(1, 5, 10, 20))`.


## 4d) Partial least squares regression

> Partial least squares (PLS) regression is similar to PCR, but the components are chosen to explain the covariance between the predictors and the response, rather than the variance of the predictors only. It is implemented in the `"pls"` method. Again, the hyperparameter to tune is the number of components to keep, `ncomp`. You could use the same example grid as for PCR : `data.frame(ncomp = c(1, 5, 10, 20))`.

## 4e) Random forest

> A random forest is an ensemble of decision trees, each grown on a random subset of the participants, where only a random subset of the genes is considered at each split. The predictions of the trees are averaged. It is implemented in the `"ranger"` method (package `ranger`), which has three hyperparameters. You must give a value for each of them in your tuning grid :
>
> - `mtry` : the number of genes randomly considered at each split. This is the main hyperparameter to tune; it must be at most the number of genes.
> - `splitrule` : the criterion to split the nodes. For a regression, use `"variance"`.
> - `min.node.size` : the minimum number of participants in a terminal node of a tree (e.g. 5 or 10).
>
> For example, you could use the grid `expand.grid(mtry = c(50, 200), splitrule = "variance", min.node.size = c(5, 10))`.

# 6) Interpreting the selected variables (optional)

> In the previous exercises, we have focused on code implementation and on maximising the predictive accuracy of the models. However, an important part of predictive analysis is the interpretation of any *predictive signatures*. Different regression methods may have different natural ways to interpret the importance of the input variables for the response. For example, in multiple linear regression, we can interpret the effect size estimates, confidence intervals, and p-values for a test of non-zero effect size. Random forest has a metric called variable importance, which tells us the loss in predictive accuracy when a given variable's values are randomly permuted. 

> In this section, we are going to use the example of a lasso regression. When using L1-regularised methods like lasso (and elastic net), we may choose to interpret the predictors which have non-zero coefficients (i.e. the *selected variables*). We will do this in two setups : a model fit on the entire dataset, as in question 1, and cross-validation, as in questions 2 to 4.

## 6b) Variables selected in cross-validation

> There is a limitation to the interpretation above : the selected genes depend on the particular data used to fit the model. If we had a slightly different sample of participants, would the same genes be selected? 

> Cross-validation gives us a way to assess this. In each iteration of the cross-validation, a model is fit on a different part of the data, and may select different genes. With L1-regularisation methods like lasso and elastic net, we can therefore interpret the *proportion of folds in which each gene is selected*. These approaches can broadly be called *stability selection* methods, as genes which are more frequently selected are more *stable* predictors.

# 7) Sparse partial least squares with `mixOmics` (optional)

> Sparse partial least squares (sPLS) is an approach which uses L1 (lasso) regularisation on the weighting vectors in a partial least squares approach. That is, it finds *sparse* components (made from a few genes only) which are maximally covarying with the response variable. This gives a way to select variables which is different from the lasso : the selected genes are those which contribute to the components.

> We are going to implement this model using the `mixOmics` package, from Bioconductor. Unfortunately, this implementation is not available in `caret`, so we will have to use `mixOmics`'s own functions to tune the model. If you have not installed it yet, run the following chunk.

```{r, eval = F}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
  install.packages("BiocManager")

BiocManager::install("mixOmics")
```

> Note : we do not load `mixOmics` with `library()` : it replaces some functions of other packages (such as `select()` from `dplyr`). We will call its functions with the `mixOmics::` prefix.

## 7a) Tuning the sPLS model

> The sPLS model has two hyperparameters. The first is called `keepX`, which is the number of genes to keep for each component. This is roughly equivalent to tuning the strength of the penalty term, like we have done previously in this practical. The second is called `ncomp`, which is the number of components to keep.

> Read the sPLS (regression) example on the [mixOmics site](https://mixomics.org/parameter-tuning/), and use the `mixOmics::tune.spls()` function on the entire dataset to determine the best values of `ncomp` and `keepX` (again, ignore the outer cross-validation for now : the function does its own cross-validation to tune the hyperparameters). Use the standardised genes `X_mat` as the predictors and the response `y_vec`. You could try up to 3 components, and test the numbers of genes to keep with, for example, `test.keepX = c(5, 10, 20, 50, 100)`. Use the arguments `mode = "regression"`, `validation = "Mfold"`, `folds = 5`, `measure = "MSE"` and `nrepeat = 3`, and plot the tuning results. Save the plot.

> Note : there is a [known bug in the sPLS implementation in the regression setting](https://mixomics-users.discourse.group/t/error-in-check-entry-pls-x-y-ncomp-keepx-keepy-mode-mode-scale-scale-unmapped-y-contains-samples-with-no-associated-class-may-be-caused-by-nas-in-input-y-vector/1202/7), which may give you an error `Unmapped Y contains samples with no associated class`. This seems to be a problem when some values of the response are 0 : a workaround is to give the response as a matrix (`as.matrix()`) and to add a small value like 0.000001 to the response values, and the error should go away.

## 7b) sPLS in a cross-validation setup

> In 7a, we tuned the hyperparameters of the sPLS model on the entire dataset. To evaluate sPLS fairly, and to compare it with the other models, we need to implement a nested cross-validation, as we did for the other models. Since sPLS is not available in `caret`, you have to code the steps yourself with the `mixOmics` functions.

> Use the same 10 outer folds as before (`folds`), and write a `for` loop over the folds. In each iteration :
>
> - Tune `ncomp` and `keepX` on the training participants only, with `mixOmics::tune.spls()` as in 7a, and extract the best values.
> - Fit a sPLS model with these values on the training participants with `mixOmics::spls()`.
> - Predict the response of the testing participants with the `predict()` function, giving the testing predictors as the argument `newdata`. The predictions are in the element `$predict` of the result, which is an array with three dimensions : participants, responses (here, just one) and components. Take the predictions for your response and for the number of components of the model.
